## DDIM: deriving an accelerated deterministic trajectory from preserved marginals

DDIM begins with the same marginal corruption family used by DDPM, but it does not require the latent path to be the DDPM Markov chain. The source defines a family of non-Markovian forward processes whose marginal at every time remains

$$
q(x_t\mid x_0)=N(\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_0,(1-\alpha_t)I).
$$

The joint path is written as

$$
q_\sigma(x_{1:T}\mid x_0) :=
q_\sigma(x_T\mid x_0)\prod_{t=2}^{T}
q_\sigma(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0).
$$

The reverse conditional is chosen so that the marginal family above is preserved:

$$
q_\sigma(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0) =
N\left(
\sqrt{\alpha_{t-1}}x_0
+\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t-1}-\sigma_t^2}
\frac{x_t-\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_0}{\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}},
\sigma_t^2 I
\right).
$$

This expression separates the previous latent into a clean-data part and a direction determined by the noise that would explain $x_t$ under the marginal corruption. The neural network is trained to predict that noise. With an epsilon-prediction model, the implied clean-data estimate is

$$
f_\theta^{(t)}(x_t) =
\frac{x_t-\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\epsilon_\theta^{(t)}(x_t)}
{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}.
$$

The generative transition substitutes this estimate for the unknown $x_0$. For $t>1$,

$$
p_\theta^{(t)}(x_{t-1}\mid x_t) =
q_\sigma(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,f_\theta^{(t)}(x_t)).
$$

Expanding this substitution gives the DDIM sampling rule:

$$
x_{t-1} =
\sqrt{\alpha_{t-1}}
\left(
\frac{x_t-\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\epsilon_\theta^{(t)}(x_t)}
{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}
\right)
+\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t-1}-\sigma_t^2}\epsilon_\theta^{(t)}(x_t)
+\sigma_t\epsilon_t,
\qquad
\epsilon_t\sim N(0,I).
$$

The derivation makes the efficiency lever explicit. The same trained $\epsilon_\theta$ can be used with different choices of $\sigma_t$ and different subsets of time indices because the objective depends on the fixed marginals rather than on one particular Markov path. The DDPM reverse chain is recovered when

$$
\sigma_t =
\sqrt{\frac{1-\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\alpha_t}}
\sqrt{1-\frac{\alpha_t}{\alpha_{t-1}}}.
$$

The deterministic DDIM sampler uses $\sigma_t=0$. In that case the random-noise term disappears, and every reverse step is a deterministic map of the current state. This is the basis for few-step sampling: choose a shorter increasing subsequence $\tau=(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_S)$ of the original training grid and apply the same formula between adjacent elements of that subsequence. The marginal constraint is still

$$
q(x_{\tau_i}\mid x_0) =
N(\sqrt{\alpha_{\tau_i}}x_0,(1-\alpha_{\tau_i})I),
$$

so the network sees the same kind of noised inputs it was trained on, even though the sampler visits fewer states.
